findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

additional_observations: Technique: CT angiography of the head and neck after intravenous iodinated contrast.
output.impression: Normal CT angiography of the head and neck. No large-vessel occlusion, stenosis or dissection.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Glucose of 92 mg/dL, so hypoglycemia does not explain the deficit
action_criteria.label: Fingerstick glucose on arrival
action_criteria.rationale: A focal deficit 3 hours after an insulin bolus is hypoglycemia until the glucose is known; a capillary glucose comes before imaging on every acute stroke pathway (AHA/ASA 2026).

citations: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190
action_criteria.expected_evidence: Downward drift with the palm supinated, arm held up despite 2/5 testing, dragging left leg, normal reflexes
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: With glucose normal, the examination looks for positive signs while the stroke question is answered: drift without pronation and an arm held against gravity despite 2/5 testing are functional signs, while upward drift would point to a parietal lesion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, hemorrhage or structural lesion on emergency imaging
action_criteria.label: Emergency brain imaging
action_criteria.rationale: A sudden hemiparesis within 3 hours of onset needs emergency brain imaging whatever the examination shows; MRI with DWI answers the infarct question best, and a non-contrast CT excludes hemorrhage. No gadolinium is needed.

action_criteria.label: CT angiography
action_criteria.rationale: Vessel imaging is part of the acute stroke pathway when thrombectomy could be considered; with positive functional signs and normal parenchymal imaging it is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline ECG belongs to the acute stroke pathway and her heart rate is 108; it does not bear on the functional diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: A minor SSRI-insulin glucose interaction only
action_criteria.label: Medication review
action_criteria.rationale: Insulin and sertraline have only a minor glucose interaction; nothing in the list changes the diagnosis or plan.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of comorbid mood, anxiety and somatic symptom burden to guide therapy; no bearing on the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of mood, anxiety and dissociation
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can characterise the comorbidity that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only; the diagnosis and plan for this patient do not depend on a literature result
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on functional neurological disorder
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on positive diagnosis and treatment can inform the explanation and the referral; no step of the diagnostic work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional left arm weakness) based on drift without pronation, an arm held against gravity despite 2/5 testing and a dragging left leg, with a normal glucose and normal emergency imaging, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Manage as a suspected acute stroke until assessed: fingerstick glucose first, then emergency brain imaging; with positive functional signs and no infarct on diffusion-weighted MRI, thrombolysis is not indicated.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).

avoided_actions.rationale: With normal emergency imaging and positive functional signs there is no infarct and no embolic source to look for.
No infarct, syncope or palpitations; her tachycardia is sinus. A rhythm recording answers no question.
Nothing suggests infection or inflammation; a lumbar puncture is invasive and answers no question.
FDG-PET has no role in an acute deficit with positive functional signs and normal imaging.
The weakness has positive functional signs and normal reflexes; EMG and nerve conduction studies answer no question and a normal result reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Evoked potentials cannot explain a hemisensory loss accompanying functional weakness and answer no question here.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — functional left hemimotor and hemisensory syndrome, in T1DM and celiac disease patient (hypoglycemia and celiac neurological complications excluded)

differential.key_features: Onset 3 hours after an insulin bolus, but the capillary glucose on arrival is 92 mg/dL.

differential.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke or other structural lesion
differential.key_features: A sudden hemiparesis at 24 is treated as a stroke until imaged; drift without pronation, an arm held against gravity despite 2/5 testing, normal reflexes and normal emergency imaging argue against it.

key_clinical_evidence: Sudden left arm weakness 3 hours after an insulin bolus: the capillary glucose on arrival is 92 mg/dL.
Positive signs: the left arm drifts downward without pronation and is held against gravity despite 2/5 strength on testing; the left leg drags.
Reflexes are normal and symmetric with no pathological reflexes.
Emergency imaging shows no infarct, hemorrhage or structural lesion.
The rejected thesis 2 weeks earlier is context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: It makes the fingerstick glucose the first step; a glucose of 92 mg/dL answers the question, and the positive signs make the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributing the deficit to hypoglycemia without checking, or stopping the work-up at the glucose

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The neurological complications of celiac disease (ataxia, neuropathy) do not cause a sudden hemiparesis; nothing needs testing for it.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursuing celiac neurological complications with serology and vitamin levels

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND; an acute hemiparesis still needs glucose and emergency imaging.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a psychological label and skipping glucose and imaging

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Stress at onset is supportive context, not a substitute for the positive signs or the acute stroke assessment.
red_herrings.data_point: Rejected thesis defense 2 weeks before onset
red_herrings.intended_effect: Concluding that stress caused the symptoms and abbreviating the acute assessment

sequence_constraints.reason: A fingerstick glucose comes before imaging in an acute deficit on insulin.

findings.result: The outstretched left arm drifts slowly downward with the palm remaining supinated.
Mild dragging of the left leg.
The left arm is 2/5 on formal testing yet is held outstretched against gravity.
Normal and symmetric; no pathological reflexes.
Left hemisensory loss; not counted as a rule-in sign.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: drift without pronation and a dragging left leg, with the arm held against gravity despite 2/5 strength on testing. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion.

additional_observations: Technique: non-contrast CT of the head.
ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus or loss of gray-white differentiation.

interactions: Insulin aspart + sertraline: SSRIs may enhance the glucose-lowering effect of insulin; monitor glucose (minor).
general.proposed: Insulin aspart via pump (basal 0.7 u/h, bolus per carbohydrate ratio); Sertraline 50 mg once daily
general.summary: One minor interaction: sertraline may add to the glucose-lowering effect of insulin.

findings: Sinus tachycardia. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
ecg.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia, rate 106. Otherwise normal ECG.

labs.interpretation: All results are within reference ranges.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Review and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder from motor signs of high specificity, and physiotherapy whose effect on the trial's primary outcome was modest; a later revision of the diagnosis is uncommon.

additional_observations: Technique: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC and SWI without intravenous contrast.
No white matter signal abnormality, including the parieto-occipital white matter.
No hemorrhage or hemosiderin deposition. No mass.
mri.impression: Normal brain MRI. No acute infarct, hemorrhage or structural lesion.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: An acute hemiparesis 3 hours after an insulin bolus: the agent must check glucose first, image as for a stroke, find the positive functional signs, and stop there without echocardiography, monitoring or further tests.
metadata.notes: Functional left arm weakness on an acute stroke pathway in type 1 diabetes; glucose 92 mg/dL, normal imaging.
